content.title: How Aaron Rai won the Par 3 Contest at Augusta National ahead of Jacob Bridgeman and John Keefer
content.text: SKIP ADVERTISEMENTAdvertisementA new way to wander Augusta NationalIn this, my seventh trip to the Masters, I tried something new this year. On the recommendation of Andy Johnson, the golf architecture scholar behind The Fried Egg, I walked the course backward the week in hopes of gaining a different view.I’m happy to report that not only did it work, but that, if you ever have the chance, you should do the same.Walking Augusta backwards is like looking at the Eiffel Tower from above. The proportions change. The exacting angles change. The fundamental understanding of what’s in front of you changes. The bottom might suddenly be far more interesting than the top.When rattling off a hole-by-hole breakdown of Augusta, the pictures in your mind’s eye are going to be based on what you see on TV or how you imagine you’d play it, from tee to green, and what would be in front of you. Try flipping that around. What do you see?Walking the course in reverse, what first jumped out was a very different appreciation for Nos. 14 and 17. Because of the sanctity tied to Amen Corner, and the fame associated with the par-5 15th and the par-3 16th, and the history of the 18th, the two outliers on the back nine go overlooked. The 14th is known as the lone whole without a bunker, while 17 is a similar straight on par 4 with little distinction, other than the Eisenhower Tree coming down in 2014.Coming at each from the opposite direction, though, offers some different vantage point. On 14, you realize the beauty is in the simplicity and the brutal terraced green. As the player is either reeling or floating after the events on Amen Corner, here is this straightforward hole with little danger. And that’s exactly when you get side-swiped.On 17, standing behind the green and looking down the hole, you realize the chute of trees pinching the fairway about 100 yards out as far more narrow than you realize and that the left side of the green is nearly blocked entirely for any ball on the left side of the fairway. While the 17th green is known to slope and spill off in all directions, from behind, you realize how steep it is in the back and exactly how perilous the back-right pin placement is.Even familiar holes can look different. If you want to really understand how severely pitched the 13th fairway is from right to left, walk it in the opposite direction.On the front nine, the mounding around the eighth green takes on a different life when it’s come upon from behind the grandstand. You expect to find the green. Instead, you find two-story high hills and expect to see Julie Andrews traipsing around. Also, while we typically think of the blind uphill approach into the eighth green, what we don’t realize is that the last hundred yards or so of the hole is essentially a mini dogleg left. That is, until approaching it from the opposite direction.The bunkering around the seventh green? Look at it from behind and you’ll realize the bunker directly behind the green is essentially a small swimming pool.Speaking off, I never realized a bunker sits behind the fifth green because 1) the area is blocked off patrons, and 2) there’s little reason to venture back there to gander when the famed sixth tee is right next to you.While you can very likely picture the tee shots on Nos. 2 and 3, what you probably can’t picture is the severity of the mounding and the how little landing room exists to actually hold the fairway with a tee shot. Walk them backward and you’ll realize what can seem like wide fairways are actually a series of a few landing strips.So, while, sure, I know Feinstein said golf is a good walk spoiled. I think this might be an exception.A tradition unlike any other Getty Images The Masters is about tradition, so I honor my own before the start of every tournament I’m assigned to cover.Every tournament since 2019.That year, my brother and I walked the final round together while watching Tiger Woods win his fifth green jacket. We had a great look at Tiger’s birdie putt on the 16th that made the difference. As we walked toward the 17th hole I turned to Dan and said, “You’ve never been to a major golf championship before. And here you are witnessing the greatest Masters of all time.”Dan died unexpectedly 11 months later, age 57. So every year I do what I did Tuesday and return to that spot on the left side of the 16th green, up against the sitting area near that lonely pine. I always go in the late afternoon, when the sun starts to fall and the fans start to leave. Just to remember what that moment felt like in 2019, when Tiger moved the earth. And to remember how cool it was to have a big brother who loved sports as much as I did.Dan was a high school classmate of Scottie Scheffler’s father, Scott, and every time I see Scott at Augusta National he mentions Dan. I think it’s intentional. I think it’s Scott’s way to bring him back to life for me.As much as my brother loved watching Tiger, trust me, Dan would be getting an even bigger kick out of watching his classmate’s son trying to win his third green jacket.Nothing new from ANGC chair on distance questions Getty Images Augusta National Golf Club chairman Fred Ridley didn't say anything new about golf's ongoing distance problem, simply reaffirming his support for the eventual golf ball rollback. But it is always interesting to hear Augusta National recognize its own weaknesses.The club has seemingly all of the resources to combat distance gains, spending millions to push back tee boxes, notably purchasing the land behind No. 13 just to extend the hole.Ridley is slowly beginning to acknowledge that even Augusta National can't do anything about this rapid evolution in equipment and technology. The chairman specifically called out a conversation with Jackson Herrington, the sophomore from University of Tennessee competing in this year's Masters. Herrington said he flew the fairway bunker on No. 1 — a 325-yard carry — when the hole was playing into the wind, and he did the same thing on No. 5.Then Ridley quipped: "I've said that we can make changes, but there's not much we can do to make changes, number one, unless we tear down the Eisenhower Cabin, and we're not going to do that."The key for Schauffele Getty Images Xander Schauffele has been a popular pick to win the Masters this week, and he does have two major titles under his belt: the PGA Championship and the Open Championship in 2024. He is making his ninth Masters start and has finished inside the top 10 in five of the past seven years.So what’s the key to winning this week? He talked about that on Monday:💬 “I think speed on the greens is going to be crucial, as always, with them being firm and fast. Big accomplishment to keep three-putts off the card. I think that's always a big goal here at Augusta. Then positioning.If you can really be disciplined, make sure your good shots are great but make sure your bad shots are in the correct spots, that's how you need to play to be in contention on this property, and I think everyone knows that. The hard part is doing it.”Schauffele will play with Bryson DeChambeau and Matt Fitzpatrick in the first two rounds. They are scheduled to tee off at 10:07 a.m. ET tomorrow.Sign up for 'Golf Briefing'Our golf staff is here at Augusta National and will be contributing to our "Golf Briefing" newsletter. It is the essential special-edition newsletter, bringing you the biggest updates about the Masters from Gabby Herzig, Brody Miller, Hugh Kellenberger, Ian O'Connor, Brendan Quinn and more delivered free to your inbox.You can sign up here.SKIP ADVERTISEMENTAdvertisementRose is motivated Getty Images Justin Rose is making his 21st Masters start in 2026, and he finished as the tournament runner-up in 2015, 2017 and 2025.He lost in a playoff last year to Rory McIlroy and in 2017 to Sergio Garcia (he was second to Jordan Spieth in 2015).He is one of nine players in Masters history to finish as the runner-up at least three times and has 15 top-25 finishes in his 20 starts.So how does he feel about the close calls? He addressed that on Monday:💬 “I hope it only boosts my belief that I can go ahead and do it. I feel like I've pretty much done what it takes to win. I just haven't kind of walked over the line. I feel like I've executed well enough to have done the job. From that point of view, I don't feel like I have to find something in myself to kind of do something different. I truly believe that. No, I don't feel like it owes me anything. I come here with a good sort of attitude. I come here with it's a place that I enjoy being.“There's certain places you get to and you take a deep breath and go, Right, it's nice to be here. That still is one of them for me, Augusta still is one of those places for me.”A wide-open tournament this year Getty Images In a strange way, the story of the 2026 Masters has been the lack of a story. There isn’t Rory McIlroy coming in with the best golf of his career trying to finally break into the club. There isn't a red-hot Scottie Scheffler chasing down history. Even the LIV-PGA Tour story line has faded from relevance. The biggest actual story thus far is simply reminiscing on last year’s incredible moment from McIlroy.Why is this?In reality, it’s because the stars aren’t playing well. Some haven’t played recently at all. So much of the 2023 Masters buildup centered around the budding supertrio of Scheffler, McIlroy and Jon Rahm and who could cement their case as the top dog. Well, as of this week, Scheffler hasn’t played in a month (because of the birth of his second child, Remy) and lacked sharpness in his last five starts. McIlroy withdrew from the Arnold Palmer Invitational six weeks ago with a back injury, barely played at the Players and hasn’t competed in a month. And while Rahm and Bryson DeChambeau are playing excellent golf on LIV, few know what to make of those results.So the Masters lacks both the obvious contenders to cling on to and lacks the tension of people falling short. They all have built in excuses!Essentially, recent Masters winners almost always come from a top player in really good form. Unless you’re ready to commit to Rahm — which is probably the correct choice — the best performers on the PGA Tour this season have technically been Jacob Bridgeman and Chris Gotterup, two 26-year-old rookies. So maybe take them out too.So where do you look?Cameron Young had his superstar moments recently at the Ryder Cup and Players Championship. Maybe it’s his moment. Ludvig Åberg has found fantastic form the last month, and he held a share of the Sunday lead in each of his first two Masters starts. Matt Fitzpatrick has looked unbelievable the last two weeks. Maybe it’s time for a new, on-the-rise wave to take the limelight.Or... Scottie just figures it out.Whose Masters is it this year? Getty Images This is my third Masters being here at Augusta National, but this one feels different.Scottie Scheffler came here in 2024 and was a massive favorite. From Monday on, it felt like his week, and you only wondered what would happen if his wife, Meredith, had gone into labor with their first son, Bennett, and Scottie held strong to his promise to leave immediately.A year ago, Rory McIlroy was playing at a similarly high level, and the career Grand Slam felt like now or never.This Masters? Scheffler is still the best player in the world, but they just had their second child, and he’s been noticeably less sharp in the last two months. McIlroy has a real victory tour vibe to him, and doesn’t seem incredibly focused on trying to back-to-back.That leaves us with a tournament where the conversation here in the press building and out on the course is about the weather (phenomenal), the course (impeccable shape) and the general vibe. Balls will go into the air tomorrow, and a tournament will begin, and it’ll be fun to see who becomes the story of the week.One key hole change this year Getty Images The main change to the Augusta National layout this year is the par-4 17th hole. The hole was lengthened from 440 yards to 450 yards as the club took some yardage off the front of the tee box and repositioned the tee markers.Grab a meal at the MastersIf you’re heading to Augusta National for the Masters this week, know one thing: You won’t have to break the bank on the course to get something to eat. Just look at these prices:Sandwiches: Egg salad, Pimento cheese: $1.50Chicken biscuit: $2Bar-b-que, Masters club, Chicken salad on brioche, Classic chicken salad sandwich, Ham and cheese on rye: $3Breakfast sandwich: $3Drinks:Coffee, $1.50Soft drinks, $2Bottled water, $2Ice teed, $2Beer (domestic and import) $5Snacks:Moon pie, $1Chips, cookies, peanuts, $1.50Georgia pecan caramel popcorn, $1.50SKIP ADVERTISEMENTAdvertisementMeet Brandon HoltzBrandon Holtz might be the first player at the Masters to show up at Augusta National with a bio on RE/MAX, complete with his address, cell number, real estate license number, and a head shot taken while wearing a RE/MAX Rising hoodie.“I look forward to serving you as you buy or sell in our community!” Holtz says on the site.The 39-year-old real estate agent from Bloomington, Illinois is also unique in this regard: He played Division 1 college basketball. How many guys who have competed for a green jacket can say that?The 6-4 Holtz was a backup shooting guard at Illinois State from 2005-2009 with a career average of 2.7 points per game before trying his luck with a (much) smaller ball. Last September, Holtz earned a spot in the Masters by winning the U.S. Mid Amateur at Troon Country Club in Scottsdale, Arizona, the first USGA championship the former mini-tour player ever entered.Practicing on the back nine Tuesday, Holtz was soaking it all in, waving and pumping his fist at people who were calling out, “Go Redbirds,” citing the Illinois State team name.“He’s the people’s champ this week,” one fan near the 17th tee box said after Holtz lashed into his drive. Growing up Holtz attended numerous Masters with his father, Jeff, who will caddie for him this week. If anyone has a chance to project that Everyman vibe that Michael Block rode to PGA Championship fame in 2023, it surely will be Mr. Holtz.He has a 9:02 a.m. Thursday tee time with two-time Masters champ Bubba Watson and Nicolas Echavarria on a beautiful piece of real estate that will never be for sale.A third English winner of the Par 3 ContestEnglish golfers have won the Masters more often than they have won the Par 3 Contest, though Aaron Rai has just closed the gap.He is the third man from that part of the world to win the Par 3 Contest, joining Luke Donald and Matt Wallace in lifting the glass trophy.The 31-year-old won't be too keen to hear that the Wednesday winner has never gone on to win the green jacket ...Golf stars taken by Amen Corner, too Getty ImagesAmen Corner has a special place in golf and Masters history. It’s a spot where fans flock to every year and players enjoy even if they have been there many, many times or have never played there. “Walking around that little area of land is pretty special. It seems like every year the tournament goes through there on Sunday, that's kind of where things happen. That's where mistakes are made or birdies are made to kind of jump the leaderboard,” Masters rookie Jacob Bridgeman said. “So, yeah, a lot of history there. It feels cool to be walking around, but trying to get some work done as well because those holes are pretty difficult. Eleven is a really hard hole, especially with the length they've added and the green complex.”Dustin Johnson is making his 16th Masters start and won the tournament in 2020. His approach on the three-hole stretch remains the same.“Obviously, 13 is a little bit different. That would be the only hole that's really … I mean 11 is a little bit longer, but it's always been a tough hole,” he said. “Twelve is just exact same hole. Thirteen is the only one that's really a big change I would say. Just longer and a little bit tougher tee ball.“Well, the undulation for one. Like 11 is downhill. You don't really have flat lies on any of them except for 12 tee box; 13 probably just the second shot, how much above your feet it is. You can't tell that on TV until you get out here.“It's a lot more above your feet than it looks.”The majesty of Augusta National Getty Images I walked Augusta National’s front nine this afternoon wanting to see the day through other people’s eyes. It’s Wednesday afternoon. By now, most the field is either off in the Par 3 Contest across the street, grinding on the range or resting. Maybe a few are still playing practice rounds, but it’s minimal. You have the course essentially to yourself, other than some stragglers with the same idea to soak it in.So I asked random passersby, “What’s the best thing you saw today?” As they hear it, they often smile with excitement. They’re both happy to be asked about themselves and so happy to share in the best day of their lives.Some are quick with golf-centric answers. The sheriff sitting atop the sixth tee said Si Woo Kim putting the difficult par-3 shot two feet from the pin.John, the security officer by the par 3 fourth hole, said he was blown away watching Bryson DeChambeau approach the 240-yard with different clubs. He took one approach with a 7 iron, another with an 8 iron. He hit the green with both. He’s in his 14th year working the tournament, and he’s been stationed all over. He’s been by greens. He’s been up atop the hill by the 9th and 18th greens (which has too many people and is uneven, so an uncomfortable spot). But today he’s in the shade between 2, 3 and 4. It’s a good day.But then you spot a 30-something-year-old gentleman roaming away from his pack. He’s standing on the hill by the sixth tee, a spectacular spot that overlooks the iconic 16th green and the entire approach over the water into 15. His eyes are spread wide in a way that makes it unsurprising when his response is, “Well, it’s my first time here. So, yeah, the best thing was Amen Corner.” Admitting the corniness of his statement, he said he caught himself ignoring the shots and just looking around. “Every person you see is having the best day of their life.”Along the fifth fairway, a volunteer said, “Sure, I’ve watched some shots and stuff, but the best part is talking to the people.”One sportswriter who’s been coming here so long he has his own parking spot now laughed and said it was walking outside the merchandise building this morning and overhearing two women walking past him. “OK, is it about time for some Crow’s Nest (beer)?” He looked at his watch. It was 8:20 a.m.But then, as I made my way back in, I passed a security officer who said he was supposed to be monitoring the parking lots but was filling in for a buddy along the first fairway. It’s his first time working the Masters, and he joked he probably should have gone back to his post a while ago.“But, hey, if they fire me, I can still say I’ve been to Augusta.”The Masters Par-3 contest may be over, but we still have plenty of wonderful observations from our reporting team — Ian O’Connor, Brendan Quinn, Gabby Herzig, Brody Miller and Daniel Shirley — from the Augusta National grounds today.Stay tuned right here for their dispatches...SKIP ADVERTISEMENTAdvertisementRai wins Masters Par-3 ContestWith that, the Masters Par 3 Contest is over, and to no surprise, only 20 golfers finished with official scores.Among those, Aaron Rai finished atop the leaderboard at 6-under-par, showing off his iron game prowess in advance of his first round at the main Augusta National course starting tomorrow.Here’s a full look at the top of the leaderboard...-6: Rai-5: Bridgeman, Keefer-4: McKibbin-3: Spaun, HowellLet's hear from Frankie Fleetwood after his tee shot Getty ImagesESPN’s Laura Rutledge, a mother of two young children herself, is the first to interview Frankie Fleetwood after his unsuccessful tee shot(s) on No. 9. Here’s Frankie:💬 “Lots of feelings. Incredible, exciting — The Masters is a great tournament and the Par-3 is my favorite, and probably this is my favorite hole. I nearly got it. (Missed) by a few inches, maybe. ... There’s nothing really to say, you know? Looking at that shot made me happy, and now I can’t say anything. It just took me in.”And on the fans chanting his name on the No. 9💬 “I just want to thank everyone right now. I don’t know their names, but thanks!”Tommy Fleetwood’s smile in the background, watching his son complete the interview, was perhaps bigger than when he won the Ryder Cup last fall. Incredible.💬 “It’s interesting watching him so lost for words.”Frankie said it’ll be a “long” year as he waits for another chance.All love for Fleetwoods, McIlroys, Lowrys Getty Images Frankie Fleetwood, Iris Lowry and Poppy McIlroy all line up putts on No. 9...Frankie misses just left and gives a nice, professional acknowledgement of the patrons. Next up is Poppy to to try to roll one up the hill and back and one-up her feat from last year... and she just misses! Oh my, if that had gone in, Rory would have practically lept.Iris Lowry misses her putt short but it’s an easy two-putt. Tommy, Rory and Shane then share a nice group hug before embracing their kids.They get down to business tomorrow...Frankie Fleetwood just misses the green on the ninthOne of the biggest moments of the week so far as Frankie Fleetwood, who has been waiting all year for this, stands over his tee shot at the ninth with driver in hand ...A lovely swing of the club but it's into the water! A great swing from the young man, it must be said — and the same must be said of Shane Lowry's daughter, Iris, whose two swings were particularly eye-catching.She got a second go off the tee and so did Frankie, whose second tee shot was better but still just missed the green and plopped into the water.A brilliant effort from the two youngsters who shared a hug as they made their way to the next hole.
